intro.why: DP is the exact solution method when the model is known. Monte Carlo, TD, Q-learning and actor–critic are all approximations of DP that replace the model with samples, so understanding DP explains what those methods are trying to compute.

sections.title: Dynamic programming and iterative policy evaluation
sections.plain: With a perfect model, compute a policy's values by repeatedly applying the Bellman equation.
sections.body:
Dynamic programming (DP) is a collection of algorithms that compute optimal policies given a perfect model of the environment as an MDP. Its key idea is to use value functions and the Bellman equations as update rules. DP has limited direct use (it needs the model and is computationally heavy) but it is the theoretical foundation of RL.

Iterative policy evaluation turns the Bellman expectation equation into an update, applied to every state per sweep:

$$V_{k+1}(s) \leftarrow \sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r+\gamma V_k(s')\big]$$

$V_k \to v_\pi$ as $k\to\infty$. Stop when $\Delta = \max_s|V_{k+1}(s)-V_k(s)| < \theta$. These are expected updates: they use all possible next states, weighted by the model, not samples.

In the classic 4×4 grid (−1 per step, two terminal corners, random policy), the values approach −14 to −22, but the greedy policy with respect to the values is already optimal after about three sweeps.

sections.title: Value iteration
sections.plain: Repeatedly replace each value with the best action's expected reward plus discounted next value.
sections.body:
$$V_{k+1}(s) \leftarrow \max_a\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r+\gamma V_k(s')\big]$$

This turns the Bellman optimality equation into an update. It is policy iteration with evaluation truncated to a single sweep, and it converges to $v_*$ for any finite MDP with $\gamma<1$. After convergence, extract the policy greedily:

$$\pi(s) = \arg\max_a\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r+\gamma V(s')\big]$$
Value iteration
  1. Initialise V(s) arbitrarily (terminal states 0).
  2. Loop: Δ ← 0; for each s: v ← V(s); V(s) ← maxₐ Σ p(s′, r|s, a)[r + γV(s′)]; Δ ← max(Δ, |v − V(s)|). Until Δ < θ.
  3. Output the greedy policy.

sections.title: Worked example: the race-car MDP
sections.plain: A car can drive slow or fast; fast pays more but risks overheating.
sections.body:
States: Cool, Warm, Overheated (terminal). Actions: Slow, Fast. $\gamma = 0.9$.

StateActionNext state (prob.)Reward
CoolSlowCool (1.0)+1
CoolFastCool (0.5), Warm (0.5)+2
WarmSlowCool (0.5), Warm (0.5)+1
WarmFastOverheated (1.0)−10

Sweep 1 from $V_0 = (0,0,0)$: Cool: max(1, 2) = 2; Warm: max(1, −10) = 1 → $V_1 = (2, 1, 0)$.

Sweep 2: Cool: slow $1 + 0.9\cdot2 = 2.8$, fast $2 + 0.9(0.5\cdot2 + 0.5\cdot1) = 3.35$ → 3.35. Warm: slow $1 + 0.9(0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot1) = 2.35$, fast $-10$ → 2.35. $V_2 = (3.35, 2.35, 0)$.

Fixed point. With Cool → fast and Warm → slow: $V(C) = 2 + 0.9\,\bar V$, $V(W) = 1 + 0.9\,\bar V$ with $\bar V = \tfrac12(V(C)+V(W))$; hence $V(C) - V(W) = 1$ and $V(W) = 1.45 + 0.9V(W)$, so $v_* = (15.5, 14.5, 0)$. Check: $q_*(C,\text{slow}) = 1 + 0.9\cdot15.5 = 14.95 < 15.5$; $q_*(W,\text{fast}) = -10 < 14.5$.

Code example ex1 (our own run): synchronous VI reaches $\Delta < 0.01$ after 49 sweeps at (15.41, 14.41) and $\Delta<10^{-6}$ after 136 sweeps. Sweep counts depend on the stopping rule, so quote them together with θ.

sections.title: Asynchronous dynamic programming
sections.plain: Update states in place, in any order, using the freshest values.
sections.body:
Synchronous DP computes all new values from the previous sweep's values (two arrays). Asynchronous (in-place) DP updates states one at a time using whatever values are current, including ones already updated in this sweep. Any order converges as long as every state keeps being updated.

Race car: in sweep 1, Cool becomes 2; Warm then uses it immediately: slow $= 1 + 0.9(0.5\cdot2 + 0.5\cdot0) = 1.9$, so $V_1 = (2, 1.9)$ and $V_2 = (3.755, 3.545)$, ahead of the synchronous (3.35, 2.35). In ex1 the in-place version reaches $\Delta<0.01$ in 40 sweeps vs 49, and $\Delta < 10^{-6}$ in 105 vs 136.

Asynchrony also lets us focus computation where it matters (e.g. states the agent actually visits), which is the basis of real-time DP and of planning in M13.

sections.title: Policy iteration: evaluation and improvement
sections.plain: Evaluate the current policy fully, make it greedy, repeat until it stops changing.
sections.body:
Policy improvement theorem: if $q_\pi(s,\pi'(s)) \ge v_\pi(s)$ for all $s$, then $v_{\pi'}(s) \ge v_\pi(s)$ for all $s$. So the greedy policy $\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a q_\pi(s,a)$ is at least as good as $\pi$, and strictly better unless $\pi$ is already optimal.

$$\pi_0 \xrightarrow{E} v_{\pi_0} \xrightarrow{I} \pi_1 \xrightarrow{E} v_{\pi_1} \xrightarrow{I} \pi_2 \cdots \xrightarrow{I} \pi_* \xrightarrow{E} v_*$$

A finite MDP has finitely many deterministic policies, so policy iteration converges in a finite number of iterations, usually very few.

Race car. $\pi_0$ = (slow, slow): $V(C) = 1/(1-0.9) = 10$ and $V(W) = 10$. Improve: Cool fast gives $2 + 0.9\cdot10 = 11 > 10$ → fast; Warm stays slow. $\pi_1$ = (fast, slow) evaluates to (15.5, 14.5); improving again changes nothing, so $\pi_1$ is optimal (ex2).

sections.title: Policy iteration vs value iteration
sections.plain: Few heavy steps vs many light ones; both reach the same optimum.
sections.body:
AspectPolicy iterationValue iteration
Evaluation depthFull convergence (Δ < θ)One sweep
BackupExpectation: Σₐ π(a|s)[…] (one action per state for a deterministic π)Optimality: maxₐ […]
PolicyExplicit at every stepImplicit; extracted at the end
Outer iterationsFewMany
Cost per iterationHigh (full evaluation)Low (one sweep)
Race car (our runs)2 evaluate–improve cycles49 sweeps to Δ < 0.01

In between lies modified policy iteration: evaluate for a few sweeps, then improve. DP complexity is polynomial in the number of states and actions, but the number of states grows exponentially with the number of state variables (the curse of dimensionality).

sections.title: Generalised policy iteration
sections.plain: Almost every RL method is evaluation and improvement pulling each other toward the optimum.
sections.body:
Generalised policy iteration (GPI) is the general idea of letting policy evaluation and policy improvement interact, independent of the granularity:

  • Evaluation makes the value function consistent with the current policy.
  • Improvement makes the policy greedy with respect to the current value function.

The two compete (making the policy greedy makes the value function wrong for it, and vice versa) but together they converge to the single joint fixed point $(\pi_*, v_*)$, where the policy is greedy with respect to its own value function: that is exactly the Bellman optimality equation.

The GPI spectrum: policy iteration (full evaluation, then improve) → value iteration (one sweep) → asynchronous DP → model-free GPI such as Monte Carlo control, SARSA and Q-learning (evaluation from samples, M5–M8) → actor–critic (evaluation and improvement in parallel, M11).

The catch. DP needs the full model $p(s',r\mid s,a)$. The next sessions drop that requirement and learn from experience instead, keeping the GPI structure.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Bootstrapping. DP updates estimates from other estimates (V(s′)); TD learning inherits this, Monte Carlo does not.
  • Contraction. The Bellman optimality operator is a γ-contraction in max-norm, which is why value iteration converges from any start, at a rate set by γ.
  • Linear programming can also solve MDPs exactly and is used in some theoretical work.
  • DP in practice: inventory control, small robotics planners and game solvers with known rules still use DP directly; with millions of states, asynchronous and sampled variants are needed.

code.title: Value iteration on the race car: synchronous vs in-place
code.explain: Applies optimality backups until the largest change is below θ, prints V₁ and V₂ for both variants, sweep counts for θ = 0.01 and 10⁻⁶, the optimal values, greedy policy and q* values.
mistakes: Overwriting values mid-sweep when you meant synchronous updates.
Quoting sweep counts without the stopping threshold.
code.notes: In-place updates propagate information faster, here about 20% fewer sweeps.
code.code:
"""Value iteration on the race-car MDP: synchronous vs asynchronous (in-place) sweeps.

States: Cool, Warm, Overheated (terminal). Actions: Slow, Fast. gamma = 0.9.
  Cool  + Slow -> Cool (1.0), reward +1        Cool + Fast -> Cool (0.5) / Warm (0.5), reward +2
  Warm  + Slow -> Cool (0.5) / Warm (0.5), +1  Warm + Fast -> Overheated (1.0), reward -10
"""
GAMMA = 0.9
P = {("C", "slow"): [(1.0, "C", 1)], ("C", "fast"): [(0.5, "C", 2), (0.5, "W", 2)],
     ("W", "slow"): [(0.5, "C", 1), (0.5, "W", 1)], ("W", "fast"): [(1.0, "O", -10)]}
S, A = ["C", "W"], ["slow", "fast"]
q = lambda V, s, a: sum(p * (r + GAMMA * V[s2]) for p, s2, r in P[(s, a)])

def vi(inplace, theta):
    V = {"C": 0.0, "W": 0.0, "O": 0.0}; hist = []
    for k in range(1, 10000):
        old = dict(V); src = V if inplace else old
        for s in S:
            V[s] = max(q(src, s, a) for a in A)
        hist.append((V["C"], V["W"]))
        if max(abs(V[s] - old[s]) for s in S) < theta: return V, k, hist
for name, inplace in [("synchronous", False), ("asynchronous (in-place)", True)]:
    V, k, h = vi(inplace, 0.01)
    V2, k2, _ = vi(inplace, 1e-6)
    print(f"{name:<24} V1={tuple(round(x, 3) for x in h[0])}  V2={tuple(round(x, 3) for x in h[1])}"
          f"  | delta<0.01 after {k} sweeps -> ({V['C']:.2f}, {V['W']:.2f}); delta<1e-6 after {k2} sweeps")
Vstar = vi(False, 1e-12)[0]
pi = {s: max(A, key=lambda a: q(Vstar, s, a)) for s in S}
print(f"\nv* = (Cool {Vstar['C']:.4f}, Warm {Vstar['W']:.4f}, Overheated 0); greedy policy: {pi}")
for s in S:
    print(f"  q*({s}, slow) = {q(Vstar, s, 'slow'):.3f}   q*({s}, fast) = {q(Vstar, s, 'fast'):.3f}")

code.title: Policy iteration on the race car
code.explain: Evaluates (slow, slow), improves to (fast, slow), evaluates again and stops when the greedy policy no longer changes; also checks the starting policy's values analytically (10, 10).
mistakes: Stopping evaluation too early and mis-ranking actions.
Oscillating between equally good policies (break ties consistently).
code.notes: Two evaluate–improve cycles suffice here; each evaluation, done iteratively, still needs about 100 sweeps.
code.code:
"""Policy iteration on the race-car MDP: evaluate (expectation backups) then improve (greedy), repeat."""
GAMMA = 0.9
P = {("C", "slow"): [(1.0, "C", 1)], ("C", "fast"): [(0.5, "C", 2), (0.5, "W", 2)],
     ("W", "slow"): [(0.5, "C", 1), (0.5, "W", 1)], ("W", "fast"): [(1.0, "O", -10)]}
S, A = ["C", "W"], ["slow", "fast"]
q = lambda V, s, a: sum(p * (r + GAMMA * V[s2]) for p, s2, r in P[(s, a)])

def evaluate(pi, theta=1e-6):
    V, sweeps = {"C": 0.0, "W": 0.0, "O": 0.0}, 0
    while True:
        sweeps += 1; delta = 0
        for s in S:                                   # in-place expectation backup (deterministic policy)
            v = q(V, s, pi[s]); delta = max(delta, abs(v - V[s])); V[s] = v
        if delta < theta: return V, sweeps

pi, step = {"C": "slow", "W": "slow"}, 0
while True:
    step += 1
    V, n = evaluate(pi)
    new = {s: max(A, key=lambda a: q(V, s, a)) for s in S}
    print(f"PI step {step}: policy {pi} -> V = (Cool {V['C']:.3f}, Warm {V['W']:.3f}) after {n} evaluation sweeps; improved policy {new}")
    if new == pi: break
    pi = new
print("policy stable: optimal.")
# exact evaluation of the starting policy (slow everywhere): V(C) = 1/(1-0.9) = 10; V(W) = (1 + 0.45*10)/(1 - 0.45) = 10
print("exact check, slow everywhere:", 1 / (1 - GAMMA), (1 + 0.45 * 10) / (1 - 0.45))
